lines.t: Your credit card company made money from you last month. Even if you never paid a cent of interest.
lines.title: THEY PROFIT *FROM YOU*

lines.t: And the fourth way they do it is so sneaky… most people never notice it.
lines.title: WAY #4 IS *THE SNEAKIEST*

lines.t: Stick around, because at the end I'll show you how to flip the game… and make them lose.
lines.title: STAY TO *THE END*

lines.t: First, look at this number.
lines.title: LOOK AT *THIS*

lines.t: One point two nine trillion dollars. That's what Americans owe on credit cards right now.
lines.label: US credit card debt · Q3 2026
lines.title: OWED ON *CARDS*

lines.t: A record. And it keeps growing.
lines.title: A NEW *RECORD*

lines.t: And the average interest rate on cards that carry a balance? Around twenty-two percent a year.
lines.label: Average APR · accounts paying interest
lines.title: PER *YEAR*

lines.t: Twenty-two percent. Keep that number in your head. It's going to come back… and it's not pretty.
lines.title: REMEMBER *22%*

lines.t: But before we get into it… how did we end up with cards in every wallet? The story is wild.
lines.label: THE ORIGIN
lines.title: IT STARTED WITH *A DINNER*

lines.t: New York, nineteen fifty. A businessman named Frank McNamara goes out to dinner… and, according to the famous story, realizes he forgot his wallet.
lines.title: HE FORGOT *HIS WALLET*

lines.t: Out of that idea came Diners Club, a card you could use at restaurants and pay later. Many people call it the first modern credit card.
lines.title: DINERS CLUB, *1950*

lines.t: Then, in nineteen fifty-eight, Bank of America did something nobody would dare today. It mailed sixty thousand credit cards to people in Fresno, California. Without them asking.
lines.label: The Fresno Drop · 1958
lines.title: UNREQUESTED *CARDS*

lines.t: That card later became… Visa.
lines.title: IT BECAME *VISA*

lines.t: And today, credit cards are one of the most profitable products in banking. Here's exactly how.
lines.title: A MONEY *MACHINE*

lines.t: There are four ways they make money. Let's go.
lines.title: 4 WAYS THEY *WIN*

lines.t: Way number one. Interest.
lines.label: WAY #1
lines.title: *INTEREST*

lines.t: Here's a simple example.
lines.title: QUICK *EXAMPLE*

lines.t: You owe five thousand dollars. At twenty-two percent.
And you only pay the minimum each month. Like millions of people do.
lines.title: ONLY THE *MINIMUM*

lines.t: Guess how long it takes to pay it off.
lines.title: GUESS *HOW LONG*

lines.t: About nineteen years.
lines.label: Paying only the minimum
lines.title: TO PAY IT *OFF*
lines.source: Example: min = interest + 1% of balance, $25 floor

lines.t: And the interest? More than eight thousand dollars. More than what you borrowed.
lines.title: WHAT YOU *REALLY* PAY

lines.t: Now watch what happens if you pay two hundred dollars a month instead.
lines.title: NOW *WATCH THIS*

lines.t: Done in under three years. Around eighteen hundred in interest. Same debt. Six thousand dollars saved.
lines.title: TOTAL *INTEREST*

lines.t: That's why the minimum payment looks so friendly. It's not there to help you. It's there to keep the balance alive.
lines.title: THE MINIMUM IS *BAIT*

lines.t: Oh, and one more interest trap. Watch out for deferred interest deals. No interest if paid in full in twelve months.
lines.title: "NO INTEREST" *DEALS*
lines.sub: if paid in full in 12 months…

lines.t: Sounds great. But if you still owe even a little on the last day, many of these deals charge you all the interest from day one. Retroactively.
lines.title: DEFERRED INTEREST

lines.t: The government's own consumer finance agency warns about this. Always read whether it says deferred interest… or zero percent APR. They're not the same.
But interest isn't even their only trick. Because even if you pay in full… they still get paid.
lines.title: BUT WAIT…

lines.t: Way number two. Swipe fees.
lines.label: WAY #2
lines.title: SWIPE *FEES*

lines.t: Every time you tap your card, the store pays a fee. Usually a couple of percent.
lines.title: YOUR $100 PURCHASE

lines.t: A couple of percent sounds tiny. Now multiply it by every purchase in America.
lines.title: NOW *MULTIPLY IT*

lines.t: One hundred ninety-eight billion dollars. In fees. In just one year.
lines.label: US card swipe fees · 2025
lines.title: IN ONE *YEAR*

lines.t: So who really pays it? Stores raise prices to cover it. Which means… you do. Even if you pay with cash.
lines.title: WHO *REALLY* PAYS?

lines.t: A Boston Fed study estimated each cash-paying household was paying about one hundred forty-nine dollars a year… to help fund other people's card rewards.
lines.label: Paid yearly by cash-using households
lines.title: FOR *OTHERS'* REWARDS

lines.t: Yep. Your free cashback isn't really free.
lines.title: "FREE" *CASHBACK?*

lines.t: Quick myth busting while we're here. Many people think carrying a balance helps your credit score. It doesn't. Paying in full is just as good for your score… and free.
lines.title: MYTH: *CARRY A BALANCE*
lines.sub: ✗ It does NOT help your score

lines.t: What actually matters most for your FICO score? Paying on time is the biggest factor. Then how much of your limit you use.
lines.title: WHAT BUILDS YOUR *SCORE*

lines.t: Way number three is the one that hurts the most when it hits. Fees.
lines.label: WAY #3
lines.title: THE *FEES*

lines.t: Late fees. Annual fees. Cash advance fees. Foreign transaction fees. Balance transfer fees.
lines.title: THE FEE *MENU*

lines.t: The worst one? The cash advance. A fee upfront, a higher rate, and interest from day one.
If you remember one thing from this part: never use your credit card at an ATM.
lines.title: NEVER AT *THE ATM*

lines.t: And here's a question that tells you who really pays for the rewards. Who do you think the banks love more? People who pay in full… or people who carry a balance?
Exactly. In the industry, people who carry a balance are often the most profitable customers. People who pay in full get the perks almost for free.
Okay. Now the sneaky one. The one I promised at the beginning.
lines.title: THE *SNEAKY ONE*

lines.t: Way number four. Your own brain.
lines.label: WAY #4
lines.title: YOUR *BRAIN*

lines.t: Researchers at MIT ran an experiment. People bid on sold-out basketball tickets.
lines.title: THE MIT *EXPERIMENT*

lines.t: Half of them had to pay cash. The other half, with a credit card.
The card group was willing to pay way more. In some cases, about double.
lines.title: WILLING TO *PAY*

lines.t: Same tickets. Same people. Just a different way to pay.
lines.title: SAME *TICKETS*

lines.t: It's called the pain of paying. Cash hurts. A card barely registers. And tapping your phone? Even less.
lines.title: THE PAIN OF *PAYING*

lines.t: Add rewards on top, and spending starts to feel like winning.
lines.title: SPENDING FEELS LIKE *WINNING*

lines.t: But wait. What about rewards? Points, miles, cashback. Aren't those free money? Let's do the math. Pause and guess before I show you.
lines.label: BONUS ROUND
lines.title: ARE REWARDS *WORTH IT?*

lines.t: Say you spend fifteen hundred dollars a month on a card with two percent cashback.
That's three hundred sixty dollars a year in rewards. Nice.
lines.label: 2% of $1,500 × 12 months
lines.title: IN *REWARDS*

lines.t: Now imagine you carry that fifteen hundred as a balance at twenty-two percent. That's about twenty-eight dollars of interest… every month.
lines.label: Interest per month on $1,500 at 22%
lines.title: EVERY *MONTH*

lines.t: Carry it all year, and you pay around three hundred thirty-five dollars in interest. Almost all your rewards… gone.
lines.title: REWARDS VS *INTEREST*

lines.t: And that's with just one month of spending as a balance. Carry more, and you're paying the bank to give you points.
lines.title: PAYING FOR *POINTS*

lines.t: So rewards are only free money for one type of person: the one who pays in full every single month.
lines.title: ONLY IF YOU *PAY IN FULL*

lines.t: Another quick trap: your statement balance versus your current balance. To avoid interest, you need to pay the statement balance by the due date. Not just the minimum.
And if a payment is thirty days late, it can be reported to the credit bureaus. That can hit your score for years.
lines.label: Late payments can be reported after
lines.title: LATE = *REPORTED*

lines.t: Quick question before the dark side. Which card should you actually have? There are three main types.
lines.label: QUICK GUIDE
lines.title: WHICH CARD *FOR YOU?*

lines.t: Cashback cards. Simple. A small percent back on what you spend. Best for most people who pay in full.
lines.title: 1 · *CASHBACK*

lines.t: Travel cards. Points and miles, often with an annual fee. Only worth it if you travel a lot and actually use the perks.
lines.title: 2 · *TRAVEL*
lines.sub: only if you use the perks

lines.t: And secured cards. You put down a deposit, and that becomes your limit. They're made to build or rebuild credit.
lines.title: 3 · *SECURED*

lines.t: And the best card of all? The one you pay in full every month. No matter the logo.
lines.title: THE *BEST* CARD
lines.sub: the one you pay in full

lines.t: And what happens if you just… stop paying? A lot of people wonder this. Here's the timeline.
lines.label: THE DARK SIDE
lines.title: WHAT IF YOU *DON'T PAY?*

lines.t: First, late fees. And on many cards, a penalty rate kicks in. Often close to thirty percent.
lines.label: A common penalty APR
lines.title: PENALTY *RATE*

lines.t: After about thirty days, the late payment can show up on your credit report.
lines.title: DAY 30 · *CREDIT REPORT*

lines.t: After around six months of no payments, banks usually charge off the debt. That doesn't mean it's forgiven. It's often sold or sent to collections.
lines.title: DAY 180 · *CHARGE-OFF*

lines.t: And negative marks like that can stay on your credit report for up to seven years. Making it harder to rent, borrow or even get some jobs.
lines.label: Negative marks can stay up to
lines.title: ON YOUR *REPORT*

lines.t: So if you're struggling, the best move is to call the bank early. Many offer hardship plans. Waiting only makes it worse.
lines.title: CALL *EARLY*

lines.t: Okay. You've seen all their tricks. Now let's turn the tables.
lines.title: NOW, *YOUR* TURN

lines.t: So now you know how they win. Here's how you make them lose.
lines.label: THE PLAYBOOK
lines.title: MAKE THEM *LOSE*

lines.t: Rule one. Pay the full statement balance. Every month.
lines.title: 1 · PAY *IN FULL*

lines.t: On most cards, that means zero interest on purchases. Thanks to the grace period.
lines.label: Interest on purchases if paid in full
lines.title: *ZERO*

lines.t: Rule two. Turn on autopay, at least for the minimum. One late payment can cost you a fee and hurt your credit score.
lines.title: 2 · *AUTOPAY* ON

lines.t: Rule three. Got debt? Attack the highest interest rate first. Mathematically, that saves you the most.
lines.title: 3 · PAY IN *THIS ORDER*

lines.t: Rule four. Call and ask for a lower rate. It costs nothing to ask.
lines.title: 4 · JUST *ASK*

lines.t: Bonus for rule three: a zero percent balance transfer can buy you time. Just know there's usually a transfer fee, often three to five percent, and a deadline.
lines.title: BONUS · *0% TRANSFER*
lines.sub: watch the fee and the deadline

lines.t: Rule five, part one: keep your card balance well below your limit. Many experts suggest staying under thirty percent. Lower is even better for your score.
lines.title: KEEP USAGE *LOW*

lines.t: And rule five. Decide the amount before you shop. That brings back the pain of paying… on purpose.
lines.title: 5 · SET THE *NUMBER FIRST*

lines.t: Do this, and the bank pays you rewards… while you pay them nothing.
So tell me: do you pay your card in full every month? Be honest. And subscribe, because next I'll show you why the casino always wins… and the trick they use to make you stay.
lines.title: DO YOU PAY *IN FULL?*
